Primary.text: What did most steam engines burn to heat the water in their boilers?
Primary.explanation: Burning coal heated water into steam, which pushed the pistons.

Primary.text: Besides coal, what did a steam engine need to take on often at stations?
Primary.explanation: Steam is made by boiling water, so engines needed regular refills.

Primary.text: In 1804, Richard Trevithick's steam locomotive ran on a tramway in which country?
Primary.explanation: Trevithick's engine ran at Penydarren in South Wales.

Primary.text: Which engine pulled the first train on the Stockton and Darlington Railway in 1825?
Primary.explanation: Locomotion No. 1 hauled the opening train in 1825.

Primary.text: Before railways, heavy goods were often carried on narrow boats along...
Primary.explanation: Canals were Britain's main way to move heavy goods before railways.

Primary.text: What did the Romans build across Britain that were famously long and straight?
Primary.explanation: Roman roads linked towns and forts across Britain.

Primary.text: Which Roman emperor ordered a great wall to be built across northern England?
Primary.explanation: Hadrian's Wall was begun around AD 122.

Primary.text: What did the Romans call the town that became London?
Primary.explanation: The Romans founded Londinium on the River Thames.

Primary.text: Which language did the ancient Romans speak?
Primary.explanation: Latin was the language of ancient Rome.

Primary.text: In which year did the Great Fire of London happen?
Primary.explanation: The Great Fire burned for several days in September 1666.

Primary.text: Where did the Great Fire of London start?
options: In a bakery on Pudding Lane
In a ship on the Thames
In a church on Bread Street
Primary.correctAnswer: In a bakery on Pudding Lane
Primary.explanation: The fire began in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane.

Primary.text: Which man wrote a famous diary describing the Great Fire of London?
Primary.explanation: Samuel Pepys recorded the fire in his diary.

Primary.text: The Vikings came to Britain from which part of Europe?
Primary.explanation: Vikings came from lands such as Norway, Denmark and Sweden.

Primary.text: What were the Vikings' long, narrow wooden ships called?
Primary.explanation: Viking longships could sail on seas and up rivers.

Primary.text: What is the name of the water-filled ditch dug around some castles?
Primary.explanation: A moat made it harder for attackers to reach the walls.

Primary.text: What was the strongest, safest tower in the middle of a castle called?
Primary.explanation: The keep was the castle's last line of defence.

Primary.text: A young helper who looked after a knight's armour and horse while training was called a...
Primary.explanation: A squire served a knight while learning to become one.

Primary.text: What did knights wear to protect themselves in battle?
Primary.explanation: Knights wore chain mail or metal plate armour.

Primary.text: Which long embroidered cloth tells the story of the Battle of Hastings?
Primary.explanation: The Bayeux Tapestry shows the Norman Conquest of 1066 in pictures.

Primary.text: How many wives did King Henry VIII have?
Primary.explanation: Henry VIII married six times.

Primary.text: Queen Elizabeth I was the daughter of which king?
Primary.explanation: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn.

Primary.text: Which November celebration remembers the Gunpowder Plot of 1605?
Primary.explanation: Bonfire Night on 5 November recalls Guy Fawkes and the plot.

Primary.text: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
Primary.explanation: Ancient Egyptian rulers were known as pharaohs.

Primary.text: Why did the ancient Egyptians build the great pyramids?
Primary.explanation: The pyramids were built as burial places for kings.

Primary.text: Which Egyptian boy king's tomb was discovered by Howard Carter in 1922?
Primary.explanation: Tutankhamun's tomb was found full of treasure in 1922.

Primary.text: In which country did the Olympic Games begin long ago?
Primary.explanation: The ancient Olympics were held at Olympia in Greece.

Primary.text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
Primary.explanation: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969.

Primary.text: In 1903, the Wright brothers were the first to fly what kind of machine?
Primary.explanation: The Wright brothers' Flyer made the first powered flight in 1903.

Primary.text: Which ocean did Christopher Columbus sail across in 1492?
Primary.explanation: Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Caribbean.

Primary.text: Which explorer's team was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
Primary.explanation: Amundsen's Norwegian team reached the South Pole in December 1911.

Primary.text: In 1770, Captain James Cook sailed along and mapped the east coast of which land?
Primary.explanation: Cook charted Australia's east coast in 1770.

Primary.text: Which nurse was known as 'The Lady with the Lamp'?
Primary.explanation: She checked on sick soldiers at night carrying a lamp.

Primary.text: Which fossil hunter found amazing sea reptile fossils at Lyme Regis in the 1800s?
Primary.explanation: Mary Anning's discoveries helped scientists learn about prehistoric life.

Primary.text: Who is usually credited with inventing the telephone in 1876?
Primary.explanation: Bell received a patent for the telephone in 1876.

Primary.text: Which woman led a famous campaign for women to get the vote in Britain?
Primary.explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst led the suffragette movement.

Primary.text: The Penny Black, first used in 1840, was the world's first...
Primary.explanation: The Penny Black let people prepay for posting letters.

Primary.text: Which dangerous job did some poor Victorian children do inside chimneys?
Primary.explanation: Small children were sent up chimneys to clean them, until laws stopped it.

Primary.text: Before electric lights, how did most people light their homes at night?
Primary.explanation: Homes were lit with candles, oil lamps and later gas lights.

Primary.text: Stonehenge was built long ago by people living in which age?
Primary.explanation: Stonehenge was begun around 5,000 years ago in the Stone Age.

Primary.text: Long ago, how did many people wash clothes before washing machines?
options: By hand with a washboard and tub
Primary.correctAnswer: By hand with a washboard and tub
Primary.explanation: Clothes were scrubbed by hand and squeezed through a mangle.

Secondary.text: In which year did the Stockton and Darlington Railway open?
Secondary.explanation: It opened on 27 September 1825 as a public railway using steam.

Secondary.text: In which year did the Liverpool and Manchester Railway open?
Secondary.explanation: It opened in 1830 as the first inter-city steam railway.

Secondary.text: Which politician was fatally injured by the Rocket at the Liverpool and Manchester Railway's opening?
Secondary.explanation: Huskisson was struck by Rocket on the opening day in 1830.

Secondary.text: What was the width of the 'standard gauge' used on most British railways?
Secondary.explanation: Stephenson's 4 ft 8½ in gauge became the British standard.

Secondary.text: What was the width of Brunel's broad gauge on the Great Western Railway?
Secondary.explanation: Brunel chose a 7 ft ¼ in gauge for speed and stability.

Secondary.text: In which year did the Great Western Railway finally end its broad gauge?
Secondary.explanation: The last broad gauge lines were converted in May 1892.

Secondary.text: Which London terminus was built for Brunel's Great Western Railway?
Secondary.explanation: Paddington station is the GWR's London terminus.

Secondary.text: Brunel's suspension bridge across the Avon Gorge is in which city?
Secondary.explanation: The Clifton Suspension Bridge spans the Avon Gorge in Bristol.

Secondary.text: Which Brunel ship, launched in 1843, combined an iron hull with a screw propeller?
Secondary.explanation: SS Great Britain was the first iron, screw-driven ship to cross the Atlantic.

Secondary.text: In 1923, most of Britain's railway companies were grouped into how many large companies?
Secondary.explanation: The 'Big Four' were the GWR, LMS, LNER and Southern Railway.

Secondary.text: Mallard was built by which of the 'Big Four' railway companies?
Secondary.explanation: Mallard was an LNER A4 class locomotive.

Secondary.text: Which engineer designed both Flying Scotsman and Mallard?
Secondary.explanation: Gresley was the LNER's Chief Mechanical Engineer.

Secondary.text: What top speed did Mallard reach in its 1938 record run?
Secondary.explanation: Mallard reached 126 mph on 3 July 1938.

Secondary.text: The Flying Scotsman express service linked London with which city?
Secondary.explanation: The service ran between London King's Cross and Edinburgh.

Secondary.text: The Beeching report that led to many railway closures was published in which year?
Secondary.explanation: 'The Reshaping of British Railways' appeared in 1963.

Secondary.text: In which year did regular steam-hauled trains end on British Railways' main lines?
Secondary.explanation: The last BR steam passenger trains ran in August 1968.

Secondary.text: Railways helped all of Britain set its clocks to the same time, based on...
Secondary.explanation: 'Railway time' used Greenwich Mean Time across the country.

Secondary.text: Who invented the spinning jenny in the 1760s?
Secondary.explanation: Hargreaves' spinning jenny let one worker spin many threads at once.

Secondary.text: Which inventor developed the water frame and built early cotton mills?
Secondary.explanation: Arkwright's water frame used water power to spin cotton.

Secondary.text: The world's first major cast-iron bridge, opened in 1779, stands in which English county?
Secondary.explanation: The Iron Bridge crosses the River Severn at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire.

Secondary.text: Which group of workers smashed new machines in the early 1800s to protest about their jobs?
Secondary.explanation: Luddites were textile workers who feared machines would replace them.

Secondary.text: Which object helped scholars finally read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
Secondary.explanation: It carried the same text in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek.

Secondary.text: Which ancient Greek city is known as the birthplace of democracy?
Secondary.explanation: Citizens of Athens voted on laws in their assembly.

Secondary.text: In which year was Julius Caesar assassinated?
Secondary.explanation: Caesar was killed on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

Secondary.text: Under which emperor did the Romans invade Britain in AD 43?
Secondary.explanation: Emperor Claudius launched the Roman conquest of Britain in AD 43.

Secondary.text: Which king agreed to Magna Carta in 1215?
Secondary.explanation: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215.

Secondary.text: Which English king was defeated at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
Secondary.explanation: Harold II lost to William of Normandy at Hastings.

Secondary.text: Which great survey of England was ordered by William the Conqueror and completed in 1086?
Secondary.explanation: The Domesday Book recorded land and property across England.

Secondary.text: In which country did Johannes Gutenberg develop his printing press around 1440?
Secondary.explanation: Gutenberg worked in Mainz, in what is now Germany.

Secondary.text: Who set up the first printing press in England in 1476?
Secondary.explanation: Caxton set up his press at Westminster in 1476.

Secondary.text: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
Secondary.explanation: The Renaissance began in Italian cities such as Florence.

Secondary.text: Which Renaissance artist painted the Mona Lisa?
Secondary.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s.

Secondary.text: Which explorer reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498?
Secondary.explanation: Vasco da Gama opened a sea route from Europe to India.

Secondary.text: Whose expedition of 1519–1522 was the first to sail all the way around the world?
Secondary.explanation: Magellan died on the way, but his expedition completed the voyage.

Secondary.text: In which year did the First World War end?
Secondary.explanation: The Armistice was signed on 11 November 1918.

Secondary.text: During the Second World War, moving British children from cities to the countryside for safety was called...
Secondary.explanation: Many children were evacuated to the countryside from 1939.

Secondary.text: Which space mission first landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969?
Secondary.explanation: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

Secondary.text: What was the title of the first Railway Series book, published in 1945?
Secondary.explanation: The Three Railway Engines was the first book, in 1945.

Secondary.text: In the Railway Series, the Island of Sodor lies between Barrow-in-Furness and...
Secondary.explanation: Awdry placed Sodor in the Irish Sea near Barrow-in-Furness.

Secondary.text: Who continued writing the Railway Series after the Rev. W. Awdry retired?
Secondary.explanation: Christopher Awdry wrote further books from 1983.
